newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thousands of German miners protest against cuts.
newsitem.headline: Thousands of German miners protest against cuts.

text.p: Enraged by government plans to cut coal subsidies, thousands of pit workers took to the streets across Germany's mining regions on Monday and converged on Bonn to protest outside the ruling parties' offices.

It was the third day of action since Bonn said last week it would cut subsidies to 3.8 billion marks ($2.2 billion) from nine billion marks by 2005 -- plans miners say will force 10 pits to close and cost 50,000 jobs in already depressed areas.

Some 3,000 miners arrived in Bonn in motorcycle convoys, cars and vans, and blockaded a main road through the government quarter as well as the headquarters of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and the liberal Free Democrats (CDU).

Miners occupied town halls, pits and highways across Germany's Ruhr industrial heartland and Saar state on the French border, vowing to keep up the pressure until government officials meet union leaders on Tuesday.

"If they don't come to a reasonable agreement we're not giving in. If we don't get what we want, we'll stick it out to the bitter end," said coalminer Dieter Hausmann, 44, who had travelled from Moers in the Ruhr valley.

Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl said the government would stand firm by its "fair and comprehensive" offer. But miners, citing a previous promise to maintain higher subsidies for longer, accused Bonn of going back on its word.

"I have three children. If I lose my job how am I going to feed them? I've worked my bones off for over 20 years in the pit, if I lose my job now I'll be on the scrap heap," Hausmann said outside the offices of the pro-market FDP, the driving force behind the cuts.
"The whole region lives from coal mining. If we go to the free market we will have 30 percent unemployment."
Miners sealed entrances to the FDP party headquarters with chains, forcing it to move its weekly leadership meeting to parliament buildings.
Nearby, pit workers revving motorbike engines, honking horns and blowing whistles blocked a junction on the main road through the government quarter, forcing traffic to be diverted.
"The state should continue to help us and not break its promise. It must stop lying and stop thinking about itself," said miner Dirk Ochmann, 33, clad in helmet and overalls.
Germany's 18 pits have been at a standstill since Friday, and thousands more miners were preparing to join their colleagues in Bonn on Tuesday, the miners' union said.

"I understand that miners are afraid of losing their jobs. (But) no one has done more for the miners in Saar and Ruhr than Helmut Kohl and the CDU," said CDU general secretary Peter Hintze, whose office was picketed by miners.

But Kohl's junior coalition partner, the FDP, was less conciliatory. Its economic spokesman in parliament, Paul Friedhoff, argued that the proposed cuts were "generous" and that the government had not been tough enough.

FDP general secretary Guido Westerwelle blamed opposition Social Democrats (SPD) for high unemployment in the key coal mining states of North Rhine-Westphalia and Saar, which the SPD ruled, and for failing to restructure industry there.

The SPD boycotted talks with the government on planned tax reforms last week in protest at the planned cuts, and said future cooperation would depend on the outcome of Tuesday's meeting between union leaders and government officials.
In the Ruhr valley town of Duisburg, around 2,000 miners from the Walsum colliery drove in convoy to the town labour office, and in Bottrop around 2,000 miners protested outside the local CDU office.
In the Saar region, miners continued to block a motorway which is Germany's main route to Luxembourg. ($ = 1.707 German Marks)
